name: Kinesis Data Streams
oneLiner: Real-time, ordered event streaming for high-throughput ingestion.
whatItIs: Kinesis Data Streams is AWS's managed service for ingesting large volumes of real-time event data — clickstreams, IoT telemetry, logs, application events — and making them available to consumers within milliseconds. Producers write records to a stream; the stream retains them for a window (up to a year) so multiple independent consumers can read at their own pace. It's the durable, replayable pipe between event producers and the systems that process them (Flink, Lambda, analytics). Think of it as the AWS-native equivalent of Apache Kafka's core streaming role.

inPractice.narrative: A website emits clickstream events. Producers push them into a Kinesis Data Stream, which buffers and orders them durably. A Managed Flink application (or a Lambda) consumes the stream in real time to compute rolling metrics, while another consumer (Kinesis Data Firehose) lands the raw events in S3 for later batch analysis. Because the stream retains data, a new consumer can be added later and replay history. Kinesis is the ingestion backbone the processors hang off.

coreConcepts.detail: In provisioned mode a stream's throughput is the sum of its shards (~1 MB/s in, 2 MB/s out each); On-Demand mode auto-scales capacity so you don't manage shards.
Each record carries a partition key that maps it to a shard; the same key always goes to the same shard, preserving per-key ordering.
Data is retained 24 hours by default, extendable up to 365 days, so consumers can replay or catch up — a key difference from a fire-and-forget queue.
Multiple consumers read the same stream; Enhanced Fan-Out gives each its own dedicated 2 MB/s throughput and lower latency.
Ordering is guaranteed within a shard, not across shards — design partition keys around the ordering you actually need.
Data Firehose is the sibling for zero-admin delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch with buffering; Streams is for custom, low-latency, multi-consumer processing.

whenToUse: Ingesting high-volume real-time events (clickstream, IoT, logs) durably.
Feeding multiple independent consumers from one event source.
Low-latency streaming into Flink/Lambda for real-time analytics.
AWS-native streaming where you don't want to run Kafka yourself.
whenNotToUse: Simple decoupled task queues with per-message delete semantics — use SQS.
Rich pub/sub topic routing to many subscribers — SNS/EventBridge may fit better.
Batch-only pipelines with no real-time need — land in S3 and process later.
Teams committed to the Kafka ecosystem/APIs — consider Amazon MSK (managed Kafka).

keyFacts.label: Role
keyFacts.value: Durable, ordered real-time event ingestion stream.

keyFacts.label: Capacity
keyFacts.value: Provisioned (shards, ~1 MB/s in each) or On-Demand (auto-scaling).

keyFacts.label: Ordering
keyFacts.value: Guaranteed within a shard (by partition key).

keyFacts.label: Fan-out
keyFacts.value: Multiple consumers; Enhanced Fan-Out for dedicated throughput.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Per shard-hour + PUT payload units (provisioned), or per-throughput (On-Demand).

pricingShape: In provisioned mode you pay per shard-hour plus per million PUT payload units, so cost scales with how many shards you keep and how much you write — over-provisioning shards for peak wastes money at trough. On-Demand mode removes shard management and bills by data written/read at a higher per-GB rate, which is simpler and often cheaper for spiky or unpredictable traffic. Extended retention and Enhanced Fan-Out add charges. The main lever is matching capacity mode to your traffic pattern.
gotchas: Ordering holds only within a shard — poorly chosen partition keys break the ordering you assumed you had.
Provisioned shards must be scaled (split/merge) as traffic changes; hot shards throttle while others sit idle.
Default 24-hour retention means a slow/broken consumer can lose data — extend retention if replay matters.
Enhanced Fan-Out and extended retention quietly add cost; enable them deliberately.
It's not a task queue — 'at-least-once' delivery and no per-message ack means consumers must handle duplicates and checkpointing.

equivalents.name: Pub/Sub
equivalents.note: Serverless messaging; auto-scales without shards but is topic/subscription-based rather than shard-ordered.

equivalents.name: Event Hubs
equivalents.note: Partitioned event ingestion, Kafka-compatible; partitions play the role of shards.
